meta.title: Who really said "Doctors are men who prescribe medicines of which they know little"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Voltaire. No source has ever been produced — and the tell is that the French version appears to be a back-translation from the English. It surfaces in English print around the 1950s and was cemented by a 1968 medical quotation book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Doctors are men who prescribe medicines of which they know little'?
meta.ogDescription: No Voltaire source exists, and the French 'original' looks translated from English — the opposite of what you'd expect. An anonymous 20th-century aphorism wearing his name.

answer.label: Not Voltaire — author unknown
answer.sourceLine: No Voltaire text containing this has ever been produced, in French or English. The decisive detail is linguistic: the French version in circulation does not read like eighteenth-century French and appears to be a back-translation from the English — the reverse of what you would find if a French philosopher had written it. It is an anonymous twentieth-century medical joke that acquired a famous name.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Maurice B. Strauss, Familiar Medical Quotations (1968), p. 394

source.excerpt: Doctors are men who prescribe medicines of which they know little, to cure diseases of which they know less, in human beings of whom they know nothing.
trail: No primary Voltaire text has ever been produced. Wikiquote files it under unsourced, with the key observation that the French version ‘does not appear to be original, and is probably a relatively modern invention,’ quoted only in recent works that credit Voltaire without citing anything Wikiquote ↗.

That is the diagnostic: for a genuine Voltaire line the French comes first and the English follows. Here the French behaves like a translation of the English — the same signature that exposes other ‘translated’ fakes.

The attribution was cemented by Maurice B. Strauss’s Familiar Medical Quotations (Little, Brown, 1968), p. 394, which is the source most later quotation books copy. Earlier English appearances are reported from the mid-1950s, but we have not inspected one directly and do not assert that date as confirmed unsourced list ↗.
source.excerptNote: The English as it circulates. There is no authentic French behind it to compare against — which is itself the finding.
source.rightsNote: No Voltaire basis, so no public-domain Voltaire text to lean on. The English wording is a twentieth-century formulation of unknown authorship — nobody to credit, no rights holder to clear, and a sentence of this length would not attract copyright in the United States. Use it as an anonymous saying if you use it at all, and do not present any French text as the original: none is authentic. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire did write real medical satire — he was sceptical of physicians and said so in print — which is exactly why this sticks. A joke about doctors knowing nothing sounds like him, and once a witty anticlerical, antiauthoritarian aphorism needs an author, he is among the first three names anyone reaches for. Plausibility, not evidence, is what keeps this one in circulation.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: There is no Voltaire text to argue about here. The interesting part is how confidently the attribution travels, and the linguistic evidence that quietly rules it out.

items.why: Nothing in his works, letters or contes contains it. Every printing that credits him cites nothing — the attribution has never had evidence at any point in its life Wikiquote ↗.

Voltaire wrote in French. A genuine line would exist in French first. The circulating French reads as a modern rendering of the English, which is what happens when an English aphorism is retrofitted with a French author.

The similar ‘doctors put drugs of which they know little into bodies of which they know less’ circulates under Osler’s name and is also frequently mislabelled Voltaire. Two unsourced medical jokes, both borrowing authority.

misattribution.truthLine: Author unknown, twentieth century. No Voltaire source exists, and the French version appears to be translated from the English rather than the other way round the finding ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The triple structure does the work — little, less, nothing — escalating to the punchline that the one thing doctors understand least is the patient. It is a good joke, and good jokes need a good name attached.

It also lands differently depending on the century you assign it to. As an eighteenth-century line it reads as Enlightenment scepticism about a pre-scientific profession; as a twentieth-century line, which is what it is, it reads as a complaint about modern medicine.
context.detailsSummary: What we can and cannot date
detailsBody: Confirmed: Maurice B. Strauss, Familiar Medical Quotations (1968), p. 394 — credited to Voltaire, uncited.
Reported but not inspected by us: English appearances from the mid-1950s.
Not found: any French text by Voltaire, or any French printing that predates the English.
Variants: ‘…for human bodies of which they know nothing’; singular ‘A doctor is someone who…’
context.pull: Voltaire wrote in French. The French looks translated from English.
